claims.text: High-entropy alloys comprise five or more elements in equal or nearly equal fractions, with each element at approximately 5–35 at.%.
Nearly equiatomic five-component HENA nanoparticles can initially form a disordered, single-phase FCC or BCC solid solution.
Five-transition-metal HENA nanoparticles possess intrinsic thermal stability at elevated temperatures.
High configurational entropy favors solid-solution structures over intermetallic compounds.
Sluggish diffusion kinetics are characteristic of HEAs and contribute to their elevated-temperature behavior.
Severe lattice distortion causes sluggish atomic diffusion.
High configurational entropy, sluggish diffusion, and severe lattice distortion collectively suppress phase segregation and grain growth in HENA nanoparticles.
Intrinsic nanoparticle stability is conditional on the absence of strong chemical short-range-order driving forces.
Chemical short-range order can produce HfTi and TiZr clusters and cluster-percolation pathways in HfNbTaTiZr.
SRO cluster-percolation pathways enhance local atomic diffusion.
Chemical SRO clusters and grain-boundary mobility are precursors to phase decomposition and grain coarsening.
Reduction of nanoparticle surface energy drives grain growth.
HENA nanoparticles remain structurally stable with minimal grain growth or phase decomposition up to approximately 0.6 Tm.
Above approximately 0.6 Tm, SRO clustering and surface-mediated grain growth overcome sluggish diffusion.
Above approximately 0.6 Tm, the nanoparticles eventually separate into intermetallic compounds or elemental-rich regions.
Phase separation and coarsening are particularly pronounced in nanoparticles with high surface-to-volume ratios.
Traditional binary or ternary alloys exhibit faster diffusion, grain growth, and phase decomposition than HEAs at comparable homologous temperatures because they have lower configurational entropy.
The proposed stability model fails for particles smaller than 10 nm because surface energy dominates their behavior.
Strongly negative mixing enthalpy promotes intermetallic formation and invalidates the proposed intrinsic-stability model.
Observation of SRO clusters or phase separation within one hour at 0.7 Tm would falsify the intrinsic-stability hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis itself predicts SRO nucleation and structural evolution above 0.6 Tm, while the proposed test is conducted at 0.7 Tm and treats early SRO or phase separation as falsification. Such an observation is directionally consistent with the stated prediction, so it would not decisively falsify the full hypothesis without a specified minimum induction time.

The stated domain includes all particles below 50 nm, which includes particles below 10 nm, but the boundary field says the model fails below 10 nm. The applicable size interval should instead explicitly exclude that regime, for example 10–50 nm.
